TEACHER’S NOTES

One important correction.
A few useful refinements.

K-means does not select principal components. PCA is a separate, optional preprocessing method. PCA creates new axes that are weighted combinations of the original features and capture variance—not necessarily business importance. If your axes directly show spending and visits, call them features, not principal components.

SLIDE 01 · THE SETUP

How does it work?

  • Each point represents one customer.
  • X-axis (Feature 1): total customer spending in one month ($).
  • Y-axis (Feature 2): number of visits in the same month.
  • Scale the features so their units do not unintentionally dominate distance.
  • Choose K, the number of clusters to form (K = 3 here).
  • K-means groups customers by similarity using the features we provide.
SLIDE 02 · THE ALGORITHM

Assign. Average. Repeat.

  1. Initialize K centroids—for example, choose K customer points at random. K-means++ is a common alternative.
  2. Assign each customer to the nearest centroid using Euclidean distance in the scaled feature space.
  3. Move each centroid to the mean of all customers assigned to its cluster.
  4. Repeat assignment and updating until assignments stabilize or centroid movement is sufficiently small (with an iteration limit).

K-means produces K groups; it does not prove that K naturally distinct customer types exist. Different starts can give different solutions. Compare several runs and values of K, and use business context, the elbow method, or silhouette scores to assess usefulness. Our demo uses fixed, reproducible random starts and stops at stable assignments.

Method reference: scikit-learn · K-means · PCA
